summary: The RX 450h+ is the only plug-in grade in the Lexus RX range — the RX350h and the flagship RX500h are conventional hybrids with no plug at all — and it pairs an 18.1kWh (gross) battery with a 2.5-litre petrol four for 227kW and all-wheel drive, in $105,350 Luxury and $123,650 Sports Luxury grades. Australian reviewers rate it highly for refinement, a practical 461-litre boot (612 litres to the roof) and a charge-sustaining thirst of roughly 7L/100km once the battery is flat, which is well under what similarly sized European plug-ins drink. The recurring criticisms are the modest 67km WLTP electric range against a BMW X5 xDrive50e's 101km, AC-only 7kW charging with no DC capability, a 1500kg tow rating, and the fact that the $123,650 Sports Luxury asks flagship money for a car whose $105,350 Luxury twin shares the whole drivetrain.
pros: The $105,350 RX450h+ Luxury added in late 2025 undercuts the Sports Luxury by $18,300 while keeping the identical 18.1kWh battery, 227kW output, e-Four all-wheel drive, adaptive suspension and 67km WLTP electric range — it drops the 21-inch wheels for 19s, the 21-speaker Mark Levinson audio, the surround-view camera, heated rear seats and semi-aniline leather, but nothing that affects range or running cost

Charge-sustaining consumption is genuinely low for a 2.1-tonne large SUV: the WLTP battery-empty figure is 7.0L/100km and EV Central measured roughly 6.5-7.0L/100km in hybrid mode, so an owner who cannot plug in still gets Toyota hybrid economy rather than the 7.7-8L/100km of a Volvo XC90 T8 or Mercedes GLC 350e
The 461-litre boot to the cargo cover (612 litres to the roof, 1678 litres seats-down) matches the petrol and hybrid RX because the battery sits under the cabin floor
Lexus Australia's five-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, the hybrid battery cover can be extended to 10 years with an annual health check, and servicing is capped at $695 per visit
Unlike PHEVs that simply revert to the petrol engine when the battery empties, the RX drops into full Toyota-style hybrid operation and recharges the pack on the move
cons: The 85km electric range Lexus Australia advertises is an NEDC figure; the European WLTP figure for the same car is 67km on both the 19- and 21-inch wheels, so the headline overstates the range by around 25 per cent before real-world driving is considered, and Australian testers recorded 55-60km

Charging is AC-only at 7kW with no DC fast-charge option, so a full recharge takes just under three hours on a wallbox and most of a working day on a household socket — a buyer without home charging is paying a large premium over an RX350h for a battery they cannot keep full

The 1.3L/100km label consumption is meaningless in use: it assumes every trip starts fully charged, where real Australian tests land at 4.8-4.9L/100km with regular plugging in and around 7L/100km without, roughly five times the sticker

Braked towing is capped at 1500kg in Australia, below the 2000kg the same car is rated for in Europe and well under the 2400kg of the Volvo XC90 T8 and Mercedes GLC 350e plug-ins, and there is no spare wheel — only a repair kit

At $123,650 the Sports Luxury sits $32,000 above the fuel-efficient luxury car tax threshold of $91,661 and buys a five-seat SUV with less electric range than a BMW X5 xDrive50e; CarsGuide called the EV-only range 'relatively short' for the money and the Luxury grade is the value pick by a wide margin
